original_question: For the diffraction measure of the Dirac comb associated with a Pinwheel tiling, does there exist an absolutely continuous component in addition to the known trivial pure point mass at the origin and the continuous part already established?
target_in_paper: Section 2.3, Problem 2.3.2: "Does the diffraction measure of the Pinwheel Tiling contain an absolutely continuous component?" ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the relevant object—the diffraction measure coming from the Dirac comb associated with a Pinwheel tiling—and it asks exactly about the existence of an absolutely continuous part. It also correctly situates the question against the known background used in the paper: circular symmetry, the trivial pure point mass at the origin, and continuity away from the origin. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))
missing_details: The paper's Section 2.3 first fixes the diffraction setup by choosing a reference point in each tile and forming a uniform Dirac comb from those points; the natural choice mentioned is the point with coordinates (1/2, 1/2) relative to the right-angled corner of the triangular prototile. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))

The tiling in question is specifically a Pinwheel tiling built from a right triangle with side lengths 1, 2, and sqrt(5); this is the exact geometric object used in the nearby context. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))

To stay closest to the paper, the question should be phrased as Problem 2.3.2 and not blended with the neighboring Problem 2.3.1, which separately asks for the positions and intensities of sharp rings. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))

The established statement is more precise than 'the continuous part already established': the paper says that, apart from the trivial point measure at the origin, the diffraction measure is continuous; the open issue is whether this continuous remainder has an absolutely continuous component. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))

The context also explicitly warns that a measure concentrated on sharp rings is singular continuous in the plane, so the absolutely continuous question is distinct from the sharp-ring question. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))

If the question is to be fully stand-alone, it should mention that the diffraction measure is defined as the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation and is a positive measure on the plane. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))

The paper treats this as a property of 'the' Pinwheel Tiling because all Pinwheel tilings are said to be locally indistinguishable and to share the relevant diffraction setting. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))
refined_question: Let μ be the diffraction measure on R^2 of the uniform Dirac comb obtained from a Pinwheel tiling by placing one unit point mass at a fixed reference point in each triangular tile (for example, at (1/2, 1/2) relative to the right-angled corner). The paper notes that μ is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation, is circularly symmetric, has only the trivial pure point mass at the origin, and is otherwise continuous. Does μ contain any absolutely continuous component? ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))
justification: The draft is targeting the paper's official open problem in Section 2.3, namely Problem 2.3.2, rather than the adjacent sharp-ring problem Problem 2.3.1. The surrounding paragraph supplies the hidden setup and assumptions: how the Dirac comb is formed, what is already known about the diffraction (circular symmetry, only the origin as pure point part, continuity elsewhere), and why the absolutely continuous issue remains open despite numerical evidence. So the sharpest paper-faithful rewrite is simply the official question, expanded only enough to make the diffraction object fully self-contained. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40598-016-0046-6))
